meta.title: Nossa Senhora de Fátima — Cronologia
meta.subtitle: Chronology of the reported apparitions at Fátima, Portugal, and of what came before and after them (1881–2017)
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of the reported apparitions of Our Lady of the Rosary at the Cova da Iria, Fátima, Portugal (1917): the anticlerical politics and the suppressed diocese that preceded them, the three seers, the Church's canonical judgment of 1930, the shrine, the pilgrimage and the seers' causes that followed, and the reported cures — recorded as accounts and as the Church acts that judged them, never as events.
meta.dataQualityNote: Work-in-progress dataset compiled from public sources (see references). The apparitions are REPORTED events: this site records who reported what and when, and what the Church ruled and when, citing the ruling documents — it never asserts the supernatural claim as fact in its own voice. Reported miracles are handled the same way, and only two things attached to them are datable: that a cure was REPORTED — by whom, and when first attested — and any RECOGNITION ACT, a dated decision of the Church with a document behind it. No entry here says that a cure happened, aggregate claims are attributed to whoever makes them, and reported cures earn no rung on the approval ladder, which records judgments on the apparitions alone. The chronology also carries context before 1917 (the suppressed diocese, the First Republic, the 1911 Law of Separation) and the institutional history after it (the shrine, the pilgrimage, the seers' later lives and causes). Details attested only retrospectively (the 1916 Angel apparitions, the 'Secret') are flagged as such; dates not yet verified against a primary source carry a ? mark, and where sources disagree the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved. Corrections against primary sources are welcome.

approvalLadder.note: Fátima's approval is DIOCESAN. The judgment that the visions are 'worthy of belief' was made by the bishop of Leiria in 1930; this chronology has located no act of the Holy See ruling on whether the 1917 apparitions were supernatural. Each rung below records one authority — what it did, when, and in which document — and the page adds them up into no overall verdict.

stages.label: Parish and local clergy
stages.who: Fr Manuel Marques Ferreira, parish priest of Fátima (1914–1920), reporting to the Patriarchate of Lisbon: the Diocese of Leiria was restored in 1918 but had no resident bishop until May 1920.
stages.outcome: The parish priest questioned Lúcia within about a fortnight of the first reported apparition and went on interrogating the children through 1917, keeping notes — but issued no judgment. Lúcia records him telling her 'Não me parece uma revelação do Céu' ('It does not seem to me a revelation from Heaven'), warning that it might be a deception and adding 'the future will tell us what to think'. He kept away from the Cova da Iria on the 13th of each month; accused in the press of complicity in the civil administrator's detention of the children on 13 August 1917, he published denials in which he called his 'absence and apparent indifference' deliberate, so that unbelievers could not attribute the crowd's faith to the parish priest. Ordered by the Patriarchate of Lisbon to gather depositions and report, he produced the parish report that became the main documentary basis of the later diocesan process, seeking in it to appear 'indiferente enquanto não houvesse provas evidentes ou a Igreja falasse' ('indifferent as long as there were no evident proofs or the Church spoke'). No favourable act exists at this level, because none was issued: the case was passed upward instead.

stages.label: Diocese of Leiria — canonical process and judgment
stages.who: José Alves Correia da Silva, bishop of the restored Diocese of Leiria, and the commission of inquiry he named — which included Canon Manuel Nunes Formigão, who had begun interrogating the seers on 27 September 1917.
stages.outcome: By a provision of 3 May 1922 the bishop ordered the canonical process and named the commission; it reported to him in 1930. In the pastoral letter 'A Divina Providência' of 13 October 1930 he declared it right 'to declare worthy of belief' (dignas de crédito) the visions of the children at the Cova da Iria on the 13th of May to October 1917, and 'officially to permit the cult of Our Lady of Fátima' (Documentação Crítica de Fátima, doc. 133). This is the act Fátima's approval rests on. In Catholic teaching it judges a private revelation credible and permits devotion; it is not a dogmatic definition and obliges no one to believe.

stages.label: The Holy See
stages.who: The Roman congregations and the popes.
stages.outcome: Rome has acted around Fátima many times, but none of the acts located here rules on whether the 1917 apparitions were supernatural. The nearest candidate is the letter 'Celeberrima sollemnia' of 28 April 1946, by which Pius XII sent Cardinal Benedetto Aloisi Masella as his legate to crown the image at the shrine (Acta Apostolicae Sedis 38, p. 376): an honour paid to an image, deciding nothing about the visions. The beatification (13 May 2000) and canonization (13 May 2017) of Francisco and Jacinta Marto are judgments about two children's holiness, not about what they reported seeing. 'The Message of Fatima' (26 June 2000) is what its title says — the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith publishing the third part of the 'Secret' with a theological commentary; it cites no decree of authenticity, and the commentary itself insists that even an approved private revelation obliges no one to believe.
stages.noDocument: Searched for a Roman act ruling on the apparitions' supernatural character, and found none. Checked: the complete document index of the Congregation (now Dicastery) for the Doctrine of the Faith on vatican.va, which lists no Fátima document other than the 26 June 2000 publication; that publication itself, which cites no decree of authenticity; and the Acta Apostolicae Sedis volumes from vatican.va, where 'Fatim*' returns nothing at all in vol. 22 (1930) or vol. 23 (1931) — the years around the diocesan ruling — and nothing in the 1940 index volume, while the control terms 'decretum' and 'Lusitan*' return dozens to hundreds of hits in those same files, so the silence is the source's and not the search's. In vol. 38 (1946) the Fátima entries are the coronation letter and Pius XII's radio message for the coronation, not a ruling. Papal pilgrimages to the shrine, consecrations of the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary, indulgence and liturgical concessions, the two causes of the seers, and the 2000 publication with its commentary were each considered and set aside for the same reason: they are acts of devotion, of liturgy, or about persons. This is a record of what was and was not found — not a claim that Rome ruled against Fátima. Fátima's approval does not depend on Rome having ruled: it rests on the 1930 diocesan act above, which surprises many readers.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A series of six Marian apparitions reported at the Cova da Iria, parish of Fátima, Portugal, between 13 May and 13 October 1917, by three shepherd children — Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto. The figure they described later identified herself, in their account, as 'the Lady of the Rosary'.

facts.label: The seers
facts.value: Lúcia de Jesus dos Santos (b. 28 March 1907), Francisco Marto (b. 11 June 1908) and Jacinta Marto (b. 5 March 1910), all of Aljustrel, parish of Fátima. Francisco and Jacinta died in the influenza-pandemic years (1919, 1920); Lúcia became a religious sister and died in Coimbra on 13 February 2005.

facts.label: Church approval status
facts.value: Approved for belief and devotion at diocesan level: after a canonical process opened on 3 May 1922, the Bishop of Leiria, José Alves Correia da Silva, in the pastoral letter 'A Divina Providência' of 13 October 1930, declared the visions of the children at the Cova da Iria 'worthy of belief' (dignas de crédito) and officially permitted the cult of Our Lady of Fátima. In Catholic doctrine such approval concerns a private revelation: it permits devotion and judges the reports credible; it does not oblige belief and is not a dogmatic definition — a distinction restated in the [[cdf-ddf|Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith]]'s 2000 theological commentary.

facts.label: Contemporary record
facts.value: Unusually for a Marian apparition case, the final reported event of 13 October 1917 was covered by the secular Lisbon press: Avelino de Almeida's report in O Século (15 October 1917) and the photographs of the crowd published in Ilustração Portuguesa (29 October 1917) are contemporary documents, whatever one concludes about the event itself.

facts.label: Sanctuary
facts.value: The Santuário de Fátima at the Cova da Iria grew from a small chapel built by devotees in 1919 to the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary (dedicated 1953) and the Basilica of the Most Holy Trinity (dedicated 2007, 8,633 seats), and is today one of the most visited Marian shrines in the world; its documentation service publishes the multi-volume critical edition of the sources, the 'Documentação Crítica de Fátima'.

facts.label: Reported cures
facts.value: Cures have been reported at Fátima since the 1920s. The canonical commission's report of 13 April 1930 lists seventeen cases, each with a named physician's certificate and the numbered issue of 'Voz da Fátima' that carried the account, and describes sick pilgrims passing through a 'posto das verificações médicas' at the shrine. No act declaring any of those seventeen cures miraculous has been located, and no standing medical bureau comparable to the one Lourdes established in 1883 has been located either — a record of what was and was not found in the sources cited here, not a claim that none exists. The only Church acts on reported cures connected with Fátima that this chronology has located are the two decrees in the seers' cause, 28 June 1999 and 23 March 2017, which judge cures attributed to the intercession of Francisco and Jacinta Marto rather than the apparitions. This site records the reporting and the acts; it asserts no cure.

events.title: Diocese of Leiria suppressed
events.text: The see erected in 1545 is suppressed on 30 September 1881 in the liberal monarchy's reorganisation of the Portuguese dioceses, and its territory — including the parish of Fátima — passes to the Patriarchate of Lisbon. It is still suppressed in 1917, which is why the reported apparitions fall under no local bishop. The suppression is an act of the monarchy, not of the Republic proclaimed in 1910; the two are often run together.

events.title: The Republic proclaimed in Portugal
events.text: The monarchy falls and the Republic is proclaimed at Lisbon on 5 October 1910. The Provisional Government that takes office is anticlerical in programme, and the Diocese of Leiria-Fátima's own historical sketch describes the years that follow as ones of confiscation and persecution — the diocese's characterisation, recorded here as its own. This is the political setting in which the 1917 reports were received and opposed; the site records it as setting, not as cause.

events.title: The Law of Separation of Church and State
events.text: The Provisional Government decrees the Lei da Separação do Estado das Igrejas on 20 April 1911, drafted by Afonso Costa as Minister of Justice and Worship and published in the Diário do Governo the next day. It ends the Catholic religion's standing as the religion of the State, withdraws public support from worship, places Church property under state control, removes religious teaching from state schools and subjects public acts of worship to civil authorisation. It is the legal regime under which the administrator of the county of Vila Nova de Ourém acted against the children in August 1917.

events.place: Loca do Cabeço and Aljustrel, Fátima, Portugal
events.title: Three apparitions of an Angel reported (retrospective attestation)
events.text: According to Lúcia's later memoirs, an Angel — 'the Angel of Peace', who also called himself 'the Angel of Portugal' — appeared three times to the three children: in spring at the Loca do Cabeço, in summer at the well in the yard of Lúcia's family home, and in autumn again at the Loca do Cabeço, where he gave them Communion. The Sanctuary's own narrative dates these only by season. Note: the Angel apparitions are attested retrospectively, principally in Lúcia's Second and Fourth Memoirs (1937, 1941), not in the 1917 interrogations.

events.title: First reported apparition
events.text: While pasturing sheep at the Cova da Iria, the three children reported seeing 'a Lady dressed in white, more brilliant than the sun', who said she was 'from Heaven' and asked them to return on the 13th of each month for six months.

events.title: Second reported apparition
events.text: Before a group of about fifty people, the children reported a second apparition; in their account the Lady announced she would soon take Francisco and Jacinta to Heaven and asked for devotion to the Immaculate Heart of Mary.

events.title: Third reported apparition; the 'Secret'
events.text: Before a crowd estimated at 4,000–5,000, the children reported a vision they later described as including hell, and a promise of a miracle in October 'so that all may believe'. The three-part 'Secret' associated with this date is attested retrospectively: its first two parts were written down in Lúcia's Third Memoir (31 August 1941), the third part on 3 January 1944 — a sourcing caveat, not a verdict.

events.title: August: children detained; apparition reported at Valinhos
events.text: On 13 August the administrator of the county of Vila Nova de Ourém took the children into custody, so they were absent from the Cova da Iria, where some 15,000–18,000 people had gathered. The children reported the month's apparition on 19 August at Valinhos, near Aljustrel.

events.title: Fifth reported apparition
events.text: Before a crowd estimated at 20,000–30,000, the children reported that the Lady announced that in October Our Lord, Our Lady of Sorrows and Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and Saint Joseph with the Child Jesus would appear, and that a miracle would take place.

events.title: Sixth reported apparition; the 'Miracle of the Sun'
events.text: Before a crowd the contemporary press estimated at 50,000–70,000, the children reported that the Lady named herself 'the Lady of the Rosary' and asked for a chapel. Numerous onlookers — believers and non-believers — described unusual solar phenomena: in the words of O Século's correspondent Avelino de Almeida, the sun 'danced' ('bailou', 'segundo a típica expressão dos camponeses'). The site records what the witnesses and the press reported; it does not adjudicate the event.

events.title: O Século publishes Avelino de Almeida's report
events.text: The anticlerical Lisbon daily O Século publishes 'Coisas espantosas! Como o sol bailou ao meio-dia em Fátima' by its special correspondent Avelino de Almeida, an eyewitness account of the crowd and the solar phenomena; on 29 October the same paper's magazine, Ilustração Portuguesa, publishes Judah Ruah's photographs of the crowd watching the sun. These press pieces are the canonical contemporary attestation of the event — reproduced in the Sanctuary's critical documentation.

events.dateNote: The restoration is dated here by the bull (17 January 1918). Two other dates are in the sources and neither is discarded: 30 April 1917, when Gasparri communicated that the decision had been made, and 4 May 1918, when the bull was executed at Lisbon.
events.title: Diocese of Leiria restored by the bull 'Quo vehementius'
events.text: Benedict XV restores the Diocese of Leiria by the bull 'Quo vehementius' of 17 January 1918, as a suffragan see of the Patriarchate of Lisbon with fifty parishes; Cardinal António Mendes Belo executed it at Lisbon on 4 May 1918. The decision had been taken in Rome before the reported apparitions: Cardinal Pietro Gasparri communicated it to the nuncio on 30 April 1917, thirteen days before 13 May. The restored diocese then went two years without a resident bishop, which is why no diocesan judgment on the 1917 reports was canonically possible before 1922.

events.title: Death of Francisco Marto
events.text: Francisco Marto dies at home in Aljustrel, aged 10, in the wake of the influenza pandemic.

events.title: The Capelinha das Aparições built at the Cova da Iria
events.text: A small chapel is built at the Cova da Iria between 28 April and 15 June 1919, on the initiative of local devotees and years before the diocese ruled on the reports. An image of Our Lady of the Rosary, offered by a devotee, was blessed on 13 May 1920 and brought to the chapel about a month later; the first Mass was celebrated there on 13 October 1921.

events.title: Death of Jacinta Marto
events.text: Jacinta Marto dies in Lisbon, aged 9, after a long illness following the influenza pandemic.

events.title: First resident bishop of the restored diocese appointed
events.text: By the bull 'Commissum humilitati nostrae' of 15 May 1920, José Alves Correia da Silva is appointed to the restored see of Leiria; he is consecrated at Porto Cathedral on 25 July 1920, takes canonical possession by proxy on 4 August and makes his solemn entry into Leiria on 5 August. Until then the parish priest of Fátima had reported to the Patriarchate of Lisbon and no bishop resided in the diocese. This is the bishop who ordered the canonical process in 1922 and issued the judgment of 1930.

events.title: Bomb attack destroys the Capelinha
events.text: In the early hours of 6 March 1922 explosive charges set in the walls of the chapel at the Cova da Iria bring down its roof; a fifth charge, placed at the root of the holm oak, did not go off. The attack is attested by letters of 6 and 9 March 1922 published in the Sanctuary's critical edition (docs. 66–67). Canon Formigão's 1923 account names individuals from Lisbon, Santarém and Vila Nova de Ourém as suspected of it — his accusation, recorded here as his, and not a judicial finding. The chapel was rebuilt and reopened on 13 January 1923.

events.title: Canonical process opened
events.text: By a provision of 3 May 1922, José Alves Correia da Silva, bishop of the restored Diocese of Leiria, orders the canonical process on the events of Fátima and names the commission of inquiry (which included Canon Manuel Nunes Formigão, who had interrogated the children in 1917). The commission delivered its report to the bishop in 1930.

events.dateNote: Two starting dates are in the sources and both are kept. A single issue titled 'A Voz de Fátima' was printed on 13 June 1922 (Documentação Crítica de Fátima, doc. 65) and was not continued; monthly publication as 'Voz da Fátima' begins on 13 October 1922 (doc. 120, fl. 45v). The event is dated by the second.
events.title: 'Voz da Fátima' begins monthly publication
events.text: The first monthly issue of 'Voz da Fátima' appears at Leiria on 13 October 1922 with the bishop's approval, opening with the text of his provision of 3 May 1922 that named the commission of inquiry. The bulletin becomes the place where cures attributed to Our Lady of Fátima are reported: the canonical commission's 1930 report cites it, numbered issue by numbered issue, for every case it lists.

events.title: Canonical commission's report: seventeen cures reported, not verified here
events.text: Canon Manuel Nunes Formigão presents to the commission named in 1922 the report it had commissioned; it is read and discussed on 13 and 14 April 1930, approved unanimously except for its chapter on the European war, and handed to the bishop (Documentação Crítica de Fátima, docs. 120–121). Among the material the report weighs is a chapter 'As curas extraordinárias' listing seventeen cases, each naming the person, the ailment, the physician who signed a certificate, and the numbered issue of 'Voz da Fátima' between 13 May 1924 and 13 December 1929 in which the account was published. What is dated and recorded here is the reporting: that these cures were claimed, attested by named doctors and published on those dates. The report's own step from them to the conclusion that 'the miracles of Fátima constitute by themselves an evident proof of the supernaturality of the apparitions' is Formigão's argument, quoted as his; no diocesan or Roman act has ever declared any of the seventeen miraculous.

events.title: Pastoral letter 'A Divina Providência': visions declared worthy of belief
events.text: In the pastoral letter 'A Divina Providência', Bishop José Alves Correia da Silva declares it right 'to declare worthy of belief the visions of the children at the Cova da Iria … on the 13th of May to October 1917' and 'officially to permit the cult of Our Lady of Fátima' (Documentação Crítica de Fátima, doc. 133). This is the key diocesan approval document: a judgment of credibility permitting devotion, not a dogmatic definition.

events.title: Lúcia's memoirs written — the source of the 'Secrets'
events.text: At her superiors' and the bishop's request, Lúcia writes four memoirs (concluded 25 December 1935, 21 November 1937, 31 August 1941, 8 December 1941). Much of the now-familiar detail — the 1916 Angel apparitions, the vision of hell, the first two parts of the 'Secret' — is attested only retrospectively through them. On 3 January 1944, by order of the Bishop of Leiria, she writes down the third part of the 'Secret', sealed and later kept by the Holy Office. The retrospective character of these texts is recorded here as a sourcing caveat, not a verdict on their content.

events.title: Pius XII consecrates the Church and the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary
events.text: In a radio message in Portuguese to the faithful of Portugal, sent for the jubilee solemnities in honour of the Virgin venerated at Fátima, Pius XII entrusts and consecrates to the Immaculate Heart of Mary 'not only the Holy Church … but also the whole world torn by savage discord' (Acta Apostolicae Sedis 34, 1942, pp. 313 ff.). It is an act of devotion made on a Fátima occasion; it contains no judgment on whether the 1917 apparitions were supernatural.

events.title: The image at the Capelinha crowned by a papal legate
events.text: Cardinal Benedetto Aloisi Masella, sent as Pius XII's legate by the letter 'Celeberrima sollemnia' of 28 April 1946 (Acta Apostolicae Sedis 38, p. 376), solemnly crowns the image of Our Lady of the Rosary in the Capelinha; the crown had been offered by Portuguese women on 13 October 1942. The act honours an image. It remains the strongest candidate for a Roman act on Fátima and still decides nothing about the visions.

events.dateNote: The translation of Francisco Marto's remains is dated 13 March 1952 in the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints' file on the cause and 17 February 1952 in the Sanctuary's 'Cronologia dos videntes'. Both are recorded; neither is preferred.
events.title: Dedication of the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary
events.text: The basilica whose first stone had been blessed on 13 May 1928 is dedicated on 7 October 1953; Pius XII granted it the title of basilica by the brief 'Luce Superna' of 11 November 1954. The remains of the two younger seers were translated into it beforehand — Jacinta's on 1 May 1951, Francisco's in 1952.

events.title: Paul VI's pilgrimage to Fátima
events.text: Paul VI comes to the Cova da Iria on 13 May 1967 — the fiftieth anniversary of the first reported apparition and the twenty-fifth of the 1942 consecration — and celebrates Mass in the basilica. In the homily he calls himself a 'humble and trusting pilgrim' and prays for the peace of the Church and of the world. It is the first visit by a reigning pope. It is a visit, and it rules on nothing.

events.title: Decree on a reported cure promulgated in the seers' cause
events.text: The Congregation for the Causes of Saints promulgates the decree on the alleged miracle in the cause of Francisco and Jacinta Marto — the act that opened the way to the beatification of 13 May 2000. The case examined was a reported cure of a Portuguese woman of 'paraplegia from probable transverse myelitis, of about twenty-two years' duration, in the absence of psychiatric pathology'; the inquiry into it was held at Leiria in 1995 and declared valid on 21 November 1997, and John Paul II's apostolic letter of 13 May 2000 places the cure itself in 1987. This event is the Church act and its date. Whether a cure occurred, and what caused it, is what the act judges — not what this dataset records.

events.title: Beatification of Francisco and Jacinta Marto
events.text: John Paul II beatifies Francisco and Jacinta Marto at the Sanctuary of Fátima. At the end of the Mass, Cardinal Angelo Sodano announces that the third part of the 'Secret' will be published.

events.title: The 'Third Secret' published
events.text: The [[cdf-ddf|Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith]] publishes 'The Message of Fatima': the photostatic text of the third part of the 'Secret' (written 3 January 1944), Sister Lúcia's letters, Cardinal Sodano's 13 May announcement, and a theological commentary by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, which reads the vision as symbolic of the Church's twentieth-century persecutions and restates that a private revelation, even an approved one, does not oblige belief.

events.title: Death of Sister Lúcia, the last of the seers
events.text: Lúcia de Jesus dos Santos dies at the Carmel of Saint Teresa in Coimbra, aged 97. She had left Fátima on 15 June 1921 for the Asilo de Vilar at Porto, begun her novitiate with the Dorothean Sisters at Tuy on 2 October 1926, made perpetual vows on 3 October 1934, entered the Carmel of Coimbra on 25 March 1948 and made solemn profession there on 31 May 1949. Her remains were translated to the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary at Fátima on 19 February 2006, and the process for her beatification was opened on 30 April 2008.

events.title: Dedication of the Basilica of the Most Holy Trinity
events.text: A second and far larger church at the Cova da Iria, seating 8,633, is dedicated on 12 October 2007 by Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone as Benedict XVI's legate for the close of the ninetieth anniversary; the first stone had been laid on 6 June 2004. The Sanctuary dates the intention to build it to 1973, when the Rosary basilica was found no longer able to hold the pilgrims of an ordinary Sunday — the clearest dated measure in this chronology of how far the pilgrimage grew. The Congregation for Divine Worship granted the new church the title of basilica by decree of 19 June 2012.

events.dateNote: Two dates circulate for this decree: 21 March 2017, the ordinary session of Cardinals and Bishops that judged the case, and 23 March 2017, the papal audience under which the dicastery's own archive files it. Both are recorded; the event is dated by the promulgation.
events.title: Decree on a second reported cure promulgated in the seers' cause
events.text: Pope Francis authorises the Congregation for the Causes of Saints to promulgate the decree on the miracle attributed to the intercession of Blessed Francisco and Jacinta Marto, and the Holy See's bulletin publishes it under the heading of 23 March 2017 — the act that opened the way to the canonization of 13 May 2017. The case is a reported recovery of a child from 'severe cranio-encephalic trauma, with risk of death or of grave consequences' at Campo Mourão, Brazil, in 2013: the diocesan tribunal sat there from 5 to 13 August 2016, the Medical Consulta found the recovery scientifically inexplicable on 2 February 2017, the theological consultors reported on 21 February and the Cardinals and Bishops judged the case in ordinary session on 21 March. The dates and the acts are what this dataset records.

events.title: Canonization of Francisco and Jacinta Marto
events.text: On the centenary of the first reported apparition, Pope Francis canonizes Francisco and Jacinta Marto at the Sanctuary of Fátima.

figures.name: Lúcia dos Santos (Irmã Lúcia)
figures.role: The eldest of the three seers and the only one to survive to adulthood; as a Dorothean sister and later a Carmelite in Coimbra she wrote the memoirs (1935–1941) and the 1944 manuscript that are the principal — and retrospective — source for the Angel apparitions and the 'Secret'.

figures.name: Francisco Marto
figures.role: Seer, brother of Jacinta and cousin of Lúcia; in the children's account he saw but did not hear the Lady. Died in 1919; beatified in 2000 and canonized in 2017.

figures.name: Jacinta Marto
figures.role: The youngest seer, sister of Francisco. Died in Lisbon in 1920 after a long illness; beatified in 2000 and canonized in 2017.

figures.name: José Alves Correia da Silva
figures.role: Bishop of Leiria (1920–1957). Opened the canonical process on the Fátima events in 1922 and, in the pastoral letter 'A Divina Providência' of 13 October 1930, declared the visions worthy of belief and officially permitted the cult of Our Lady of Fátima.

figures.name: Avelino de Almeida
figures.role: Journalist of the Lisbon daily O Século, present at the Cova da Iria on 13 October 1917; his reports in O Século (15 October) and Ilustração Portuguesa (29 October) are the best-known contemporary press attestation of the 'Miracle of the Sun'. He recorded what the crowd saw and cried without endorsing a supernatural reading.

figures.name: Manuel Nunes Formigão
figures.role: Canon and seminary professor who interrogated the children from September 1917 and served on the canonical commission named in 1922; his interrogations are among the earliest written records of the seers' accounts.

organizations.name: Santuário de Fátima
organizations.relation: The shrine built at the site of the reported apparitions — the first chapel in 1919, a chaplaincy created in 1927 — today under the Diocese of Leiria-Fátima. Its documentation service publishes the critical edition of the sources ('Documentação Crítica de Fátima') used throughout this chronology. It is the official — and therefore sympathetic — custodian of the narrative; independent and critical sources are listed alongside it.

organizations.name: Diocese de Leiria-Fátima
organizations.relation: The diocese with canonical jurisdiction over Fátima. Erected in 1545, suppressed on 30 September 1881, restored by Benedict XV's bull 'Quo vehementius' of 17 January 1918 and given a resident bishop only in 1920; renamed Leiria-Fátima by the bull 'Qua pietate' of 13 May 1984. Its bishop opened the 1922 canonical process and issued the 1930 approval. Note: approval of an apparition at diocesan level is the ordinary canonical route — Fátima's 1930 approval was diocesan, later embraced by papal acts (visits, consecrations, a coronation, beatifications, canonizations) without a separate 'papal approval' decree.

organizations.name: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
organizations.relation: The Roman dicastery for doctrine — founded in 1542 as the Roman Inquisition, renamed Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith in 1965 and, since 2022, the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith. Custodian of the sealed third part of the 'Secret' from 1957 and publisher of 'The Message of Fatima' (26 June 2000), which made the text public with Cardinal Ratzinger's theological commentary.

organizations.name: Congregation for the Causes of Saints
organizations.relation: The Roman dicastery for beatifications and canonizations, split off from the Congregation of Rites by Paul VI's apostolic constitution 'Sacra Rituum Congregatio' of 8 May 1969 and a Dicastery since 5 June 2022. It is the only body that has ever ruled on a cure connected with Fátima: its decrees of 28 June 1999 and 23 March 2017 concern cures attributed to the intercession of Francisco and Jacinta Marto, and opened the way to their beatification and canonization. Those decrees judge the two children's intercession, not the 1917 apparitions, and earn no rung on the approval ladder.

disambiguation.note: Fátima is contested terrain between believers, skeptics and historians. This dataset records reports and rulings, with their dates and documents — it does not assert or deny the supernatural claim.

items.title: Reported apparition ≠ asserted fact
items.text: Every apparition entry in this chronology is a report: the children said they saw the Lady; the press said the crowd saw the sun move. The Church's 1930 ruling judged the visions 'worthy of belief' — a credibility judgment permitting devotion. None of these records, nor this site, asserts the supernatural event as established fact; Cardinal Ratzinger's 2000 commentary itself notes that assent to an approved private revelation is not obligatory for Catholics.

items.title: The 1917 record ≠ the memoirs
items.text: What was written down in 1917 (parish and Formigão interrogations, press reports) is much sparser than the now-familiar narrative. The Angel apparitions of 1916, the vision of hell and the three-part 'Secret' are attested principally in Lúcia's memoirs of 1935–1941 and her 1944 manuscript — retrospective sources written 18–27 years after the events. Recording this gap is a sourcing caveat, not a verdict on their truthfulness.

items.title: 'Worthy of belief' ≠ dogma
items.text: The 1930 formula 'dignas de crédito' (worthy of belief) authorizes public devotion and states that the reports show signs of credibility. It binds no one to believe: in Catholic teaching Fátima is a private revelation, distinct from the deposit of faith — a distinction the 2000 Vatican commentary restates explicitly.

items.title: Contemporary press attestation ≠ press endorsement
items.text: O Século was an anticlerical republican paper; Avelino de Almeida reported what tens of thousands present said they saw ('the sun danced', as he put it, 'in the peasants' typical expression') and framed 'miracle' as the crowd's cry, not the paper's conclusion. Citing his report attests the event's contemporaneity and scale, not a supernatural explanation.

references.title: Narrativa das aparições
references.publisherNote: The Sanctuary's official narrative of the 1916 Angel and 1917 Marian apparitions — the custodian's own account, sympathetic by nature; used here for the canonical dates, places and crowd estimates it records.

references.title: Cronologia dos videntes
references.publisherNote: The Sanctuary's dated chronology of the three seers: births, deaths, Lúcia's religious life, and the completion dates of her four memoirs.

references.title: Documentação Crítica de Fátima. Seleção de documentos (1917–1930)
references.publisherNote: A one-volume selection (free PDF at the linked page) from the Sanctuary's multi-volume critical edition of the primary documents: the 1917 interrogations, the full text of Avelino de Almeida's O Século article of 15 October 1917, the 3 May 1922 provision opening the canonical process, the commission's report of 13 April 1930 with its chapter on reported cures (doc. 120) and the minute of its approval (doc. 121), and the pastoral letter 'A Divina Providência' of 13 October 1930 (doc. 133). The PDF was downloaded and read for this dataset: the operative words quoted here were checked against pp. 549–550, where the bishop resolves '1º declarar como dignas de crédito as visões das crianças na Cova da Iria … nos dias 13 de maio a outubro de 1917; 2º permitir oficialmente o culto de Nossa Senhora de Fátima'.

references.title: The Message of Fatima
references.publisher: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (vatican.va)
references.publisherNote: The 26 June 2000 publication of the third part of the 'Secret' with Sister Lúcia's manuscript in facsimile, Cardinal Sodano's 13 May 2000 announcement and Cardinal Ratzinger's theological commentary — the primary source for the Secret's textual history (Third Memoir 31 August 1941; third part written 3 January 1944) and for the Church's own doctrine on private revelation.

references.title: Homily at the Beatification of Francisco and Jacinta Marto (Fátima, 13 May 2000)
references.publisherNote: The pope's own homily at the 13 May 2000 beatification, published by the Holy See — an official and by nature sympathetic source, cited here for the act and its date.

references.title: Homily at the Canonization of Francisco and Jacinta Marto (Fátima, 13 May 2017)
references.publisherNote: The pope's own homily at the 13 May 2017 canonization, published by the Holy See — an official and by nature sympathetic source, cited here for the act and its date.

references.title: Ilustração Portuguesa n.º 610, 29 October 1917, p. 353 (facsimile)
references.publisherNote: Public-domain facsimile scan of the page of O Século's illustrated magazine carrying the crowd photographs of 13 October 1917. The magazine's own digitized run at the Lisbon Hemeroteca Digital was unreachable from this session (HTTP 403 — bot filter, inconclusive, not dead), so the Commons scan is cited as the reachable facsimile.

references.title: Aparições, 90 anos de Fátima
references.publisherNote: A dated milestone list from the news agency of the Portuguese Bishops' Conference — an official-Church perspective; used for the 13/19 August 1917 sequence, the 3 May 1922 provision and the 1930 pastoral letter.

references.title: Our Lady of Fátima
references.publisherNote: A tertiary, collaboratively edited overview, cited only for uncontested orientation (the shrine's present scale); every dated claim in this chronology rests on one of the primary or press sources above.

references.title: 21 – P. Manuel Marques Ferreira (1880-1945) – O pároco de Fátima
references.publisherNote: A biographical article by Luís Miguel Ferraz (19 December 2017) in the diocese's own '100 anos – Figuras & Factos' series, drawing on Luciano Cristino's entry in the Enciclopédia de Fátima — an official-Church source, sympathetic by nature, cited here for the parish priest's reserve in 1917 (including the words Lúcia's memoirs record him using), for his press denials over the August 1917 detention, and for the restored Diocese of Leiria having no resident bishop until May 1920.

references.title: Acta Apostolicae Sedis 38 (1946)
references.publisherNote: The official gazette of the Holy See, scanned by vatican.va. Cited for the letter 'Celeberrima sollemnia' of 28 April 1946 (p. 376), by which Pius XII appointed Cardinal Benedetto Aloisi Masella his legate to crown the image of Our Lady of Fátima — the strongest candidate for a 'Roman act' on Fátima, and one that honours an image rather than ruling on the apparitions. Volumes 22 (1930) and 23 (1931) and the 1940 index volume from the same archive were searched for any Fátima entry and contain none.

references.title: A história e o impacto de Fátima, o milagre dos crentes
references.publisherNote: A long-form journalistic feature from an independent Portuguese outlet, covering the history and its critical readings — included so the reference list spans beyond official-Church sources.

references.title: Separação do Estado das Igrejas (1911)
references.publisherNote: The Portuguese parliament's own note on the Law of Separation of Church and State — a civil, non-ecclesiastical official source, cited here for the proclamation of the Republic on 5 October 1910, the law's date of 20 April 1911 and its authorship by Afonso Costa. It is the state's account of its own act and is sympathetic to it; the Church's account of the same years is cited alongside it.

references.title: 24 – Diocese de Leiria-Fátima: resenha histórica
references.publisherNote: A historical sketch by Luís Miguel Ferraz (12 January 2018) in the diocese's own '100 anos – Figuras & Factos' series — an official-Church source, sympathetic by nature, and the source of the diocese's own characterisation of the First Republic as a time of confiscation and persecution, recorded here as its characterisation. Cited for the erection of the see in 1545, its suppression on 30 September 1881, the 1918 restoration and the 1984 renaming to Leiria-Fátima.

references.title: 27 – A bula de restauração da diocese de Leiria em 1918
references.publisherNote: An article by the medieval historian Saul António Gomes (6 February 2018) in the same diocesan series, working directly from the bull — the closest thing in this reference list to an academic treatment, though published by the diocese. Cited for the bull 'Quo vehementius' of 17 January 1918, for its execution in Lisbon on 4 May 1918 and for the restored see's fifty parishes.

references.title: 19 – As aparições em Fátima e a restauração da diocese
references.publisherNote: An article by Luís Miguel Ferraz (13 December 2017) in the same diocesan series, on how the restoration of the see and the reported apparitions ran alongside one another. Cited for the diocese still being extinct in 1917, its territory then belonging to Lisbon, and for Cardinal Pietro Gasparri's communication of 30 April 1917 that the restoration had been decided — thirteen days before 13 May 1917.

references.title: 14 – D. José Alves Correia da Silva (1872-1957) – o primeiro bispo da diocese restaurada
references.publisherNote: A biographical article by Fr Luciano Cristino (21 November 2017), adapted from his entry in the Enciclopédia de Fátima, in the same diocesan series — official-Church and sympathetic. Cited for the bull 'Commissum humilitati nostrae' of 15 May 1920, the episcopal consecration of 25 July 1920 at Porto, the taking of possession by proxy on 4 August and the solemn entry into Leiria on 5 August 1920.

references.title: Lugares das aparições
references.publisherNote: The Sanctuary's page on the places of the reported apparitions — the custodian's own account, sympathetic by nature. Cited for the building of the Capelinha das Aparições between 28 April and 15 June 1919, the first Mass there on 13 October 1921, the bomb attack of 6 March 1922 and the reopening on 13 January 1923, and for the image blessed on 13 May 1920 and crowned on 13 May 1946.

references.title: Lugares de culto e oração
references.publisherNote: The Sanctuary's page on its places of worship — official and sympathetic. Cited for the first stone of the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary blessed on 13 May 1928 and its dedication on 7 October 1953, for the title of basilica granted by the brief 'Luce Superna' of 11 November 1954, and for the Basilica of the Most Holy Trinity (first stone 6 June 2004, dedicated 12 October 2007, 8,633 seats, title of basilica by decree of 19 June 2012).

references.title: Francisco e Jacinta Marto (†1919/1920)
references.publisherNote: The Roman dicastery's own file on the cause — official and by nature sympathetic, and the authoritative record of what each act in the cause was and when. Cited for the decree on the heroic virtues (13 May 1989), the decree on the miracle for the beatification (28 June 1999) and the description of the case it examined, the steps of the second case (Campo Mourão 2016–2017) and John Paul II's apostolic letter of 13 May 2000, which dates the first reported cure to 1987.

references.title: Decreti pubblicati nel 2017
references.publisherNote: The dicastery's archive of decrees promulgated in 2017, which carries the text published in the Holy See's bulletin under the heading '23 MARZO 2017' — cited for the wording of the decree on the miracle attributed to the intercession of Blessed Francisco and Jacinta Marto and for its date.

references.title: Profilo del Dicastero
references.publisherNote: The dicastery's own institutional profile — official, and cited only for uncontested institutional dates: the Congregation of Rites erected by Sixtus V on 22 January 1588, its division by Paul VI's apostolic constitution 'Sacra Rituum Congregatio' of 8 May 1969 which created the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, and its becoming a Dicastery under 'Praedicate Evangelium' with effect from 5 June 2022.

references.title: Acta Apostolicae Sedis 34 (1942)
references.publisherNote: The official gazette of the Holy See, scanned by vatican.va. Cited for the radio message of 31 October 1942 to the faithful of Portugal — headed in the volume as sent 'die XXXI mensis Octobris a. MCMXXXXII ad Lusitaniae christifideles' for the solemnities in honour of the Blessed Virgin venerated at Fátima (pp. 313 ff.) — in which Pius XII consecrated the Church and the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary. The volume was read directly for this dataset.

references.title: Peregrinação do Santo Padre ao Santuário de Nossa Senhora de Fátima — Homilia do Papa Paulo VI (13 de maio de 1967)
references.publisherNote: The pope's own homily at Fátima on 13 May 1967, published by the Holy See — official and by nature sympathetic. Cited for the date and character of the first visit by a reigning pope: he describes himself as coming 'peregrino humilde e confiante' for the fiftieth anniversary of the apparitions and the twenty-fifth of the consecration of the world to the Immaculate Heart, and makes no judgment on the apparitions. The English page on vatican.va is a stub; the Portuguese and Italian carry the text.

references.title: Radiomessaggio di Sua Santità Pio XII: «Preghiera per la consacrazione della Chiesa e del genere umano al Cuore Immacolato di Maria», 31 October 1942
references.publisherNote: Primary source, read in full for this dataset. The broadcast was addressed to Portugal for the jubilee of the apparitions; vatican.va carries the Italian text. The prayer names neither Fátima nor Russia — the nearest it comes is "ai popoli separati per l'errore o per la discordia" — and that absence is recorded here because it is the point at issue in the later literature.

references.title: Pius XII, Epistula Apostolica «Sacro vergente anno» (Ad universos Russiae populos), 7 July 1952 — Acta Apostolicae Sedis 44 (1952), pp. 505–511
references.publisherNote: Primary source: the Holy See's official gazette, scanned OCR PDF, searched and read directly for this dataset. The consecration clause is on p. 511. Fátima is not mentioned anywhere in the letter.

references.title: Paul VI, Allocution at the conclusion of the third session of the Second Vatican Council, 21 November 1964 — AAS 56 (1964), pp. 1007–1018
references.publisherNote: Primary source, read in full for this dataset. Cited for nn. 40 and 48, which are routinely described in devotional literature as Paul VI "renewing the consecration"; the verbs in the text are "affidiamo" and "raccomandiamo", and the act he recalls is Pius XII's, dated by that literature to 1952 where the world consecration was 1942.

references.title: Paul VI, Apostolic Exhortation «Signum Magnum», 13 May 1967
references.publisherNote: Primary source. Issued for the fiftieth anniversary of the apparitions and the twenty-fifth of the 1942 consecration; cited here for the fact that what it asks for is the renewal by the faithful of their own consecration, not a new papal act.

references.title: Francis, «Act of entrustment to Mary, Blessed Virgin Mary of Fátima», 13 October 2013
references.publisherNote: Primary source, read in full for this dataset. The word "consecrate" does not occur in it, and neither Russia nor the Immaculate Heart is named — which is why this dataset records it as an entrustment and not as a consecration.

references.title: Francis, «Act of Consecration to the Immaculate Heart of Mary», 25 March 2022
references.publisherNote: Primary source, read in full for this dataset. The only papal act in this series whose own text consecrates Russia by name alongside Ukraine.

references.title: Francis, Letter to the Bishops for the Act of Consecration to the Immaculate Heart of Mary, 21 March 2022
references.publisherNote: Primary source: the convocation. Cited for the collegial character of the 2022 act — the bishops of the world were invited to join it — which is the second of the two conditions this section scores.

consecrations.heading: The papal consecrations
consecrations.intro: Nine papal acts, from 1942 to 2022, are commonly counted as steps in "the consecration" the seers reported being asked for. They are not interchangeable. Some consecrate, some entrust, one only exhorts the faithful to consecrate themselves; they consecrate different objects; and only one names Russia while only two are made in union with the bishops of the world. This section sets each act against those two conditions, taking the answer from the act's own text.
consecrations.note: None of this is Fátima's approval, and the dates say so before any argument does. Fátima was declared worthy of belief by the Bishop of Leiria on 13 October 1930 — twelve years before the first act below. A consecration is an act of devotion by a pope; it presupposes the devotion rather than adjudicating the apparition, which is why no act here appears as a rung on the approval ladder above and why the Holy See rung remains "no ruling located". What the sequence does show is how deeply Rome engaged with the Fátima devotion without ever ruling on the 1917 events — and that is worth a section of its own precisely because the engagement is so easily mistaken for the ruling.
consecrations.criteria: The two columns are the two conditions Sister Lúcia reported: that Russia be consecrated by name, and that the pope act in union with the bishops of the world. They are scored from each act's own published text — "named" means the word is in the act. Whether the conditions were satisfied is a judgment this page attributes and does not make: Sister Lúcia wrote on 8 November 1989 that the 1984 act was done as asked, the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith published that letter in 2000 and called further discussion baseless, and a body of writers continues to disagree. All three positions are recorded; none is endorsed.

acts.place: Vatican City — radio message broadcast to Portugal
acts.object: The Church and the whole human race
acts.text: Broadcast in Portuguese to the Portuguese nation for the jubilee of the apparitions, and the first papal consecration in this series. What it consecrates is the Church and the human race; the text on vatican.va names neither Fátima nor Russia. The nearest it comes to the second is a petition for "the peoples separated by error or by discord" — among whom, it says, there was no house without the venerable icon in a place of honour, "today perhaps hidden away and put by for better days". Readers have taken that as Russia in all but the word ever since, and the dataset records the wording rather than the reading. Pius XII repeated the act in Saint Peter's later that year; no vatican.va document for that repetition was reached here.
acts.quote: Ai popoli separati per l'errore o per la discordia, e segnatamente a coloro che professano per Voi singolare devozione, e presso i quali non c'era casa ove non si tenesse in onore la vostra veneranda icone (oggi forse occultata e riposta per giorni migliori), date la pace e riconduceteli all'unico ovile di Cristo, sotto l'unico e vero Pastore.

acts.place: Rome — apostolic letter to all the peoples of Russia
acts.text: "Sacro vergente anno", dated at Saint Peter's on the feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius, consecrates the peoples of Russia by name — the first papal act in this series to do so, ten years after the general consecration it explicitly recalls. The pope says he acted on petitions asking him for exactly this. The letter runs to seven pages in the official gazette and does not mention Fátima once: the act names Russia without naming the apparition, in the same way the 1942 act named the apparition's country without naming Russia.
acts.quote: …quemadmodum paucis ante annis universum hominum genus Immaculato Deiparae Virginis Cordi consecravimus, ita in praesens cunctos Russiarum populos eidem Immaculato Cordi peculiarissimo modo dedicamus ac consecramus. ("…as a few years ago we consecrated the whole human race to the Immaculate Heart of the Virgin Mother of God, so now we dedicate and consecrate all the peoples of Russia in a most special way to that same Immaculate Heart.")

acts.place: Saint Peter's Basilica — close of the third session of the Second Vatican Council
acts.object: The whole human race, commended to the Immaculate Heart
acts.text: Widely reported as the act by which Paul VI renewed his predecessor's consecration, and that is not what the text does. At n. 40 he recalls that Pius XII "consecrated" the world to the Immaculate Heart, says he thought it right to commemorate that act, announces a Golden Rose for the shrine of Fátima, and adds that by this gesture "we too entrust" the protection of all humanity to Mary's heavenly care. At n. 48 he commends the whole human race to her Immaculate Heart. The verbs are "affidiamo" and "raccomandiamo", not "consacriamo"; the consecration in the passage is Pius XII's, not his own. This entry keeps the distinction because the literature that reports a renewal here also tends to date the act it renews to 1952, when the world consecration was 1942 — two slips that compound.
acts.quote: Con questo gesto anche Noi affidiamo alla celeste tutela di Maria la protezione dell'intera umanità… Al tuo Cuore Immacolato, o Vergine Madre di Dio, raccomandiamo tutto il genere umano.

acts.place: Fátima, Portugal — and Rome, by apostolic exhortation the same day
acts.object: No new papal consecration: the faithful are asked to renew their own
acts.text: Paul VI went to the Cova da Iria on the fiftieth anniversary of the first reported apparition — the first pope to do so — and issued "Signum Magnum" the same day. The exhortation is built on the twenty-fifth anniversary of Pius XII's 1942 consecration, and what it asks for is that the sons of the Church renew personally their own consecration to the Immaculate Heart. It is included here precisely because it is not a papal consecration: an anniversary, a pilgrimage and an exhortation are three things a chronology can easily let collapse into a fourth that did not happen.
acts.quote: …we exhort all the sons of the Church to renew personally their consecration to the Immaculate Heart of the Mother of the Church.

acts.place: Basilica of Saint Mary Major, Rome — the pope absent, his recorded voice broadcast
acts.object: The world, entrusted to the Immaculate Heart
acts.text: An Act of Entrustment composed by John Paul II for Pentecost, marking the sixteenth centenary of the First Council of Constantinople and the fifteenth and a half of Ephesus. He was not there: he was recovering from the attempt on his life of 13 May, and his recorded address was played in the basilica. The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith's 2000 account treats this act as the first of the series that culminates in 1984.

acts.place: Fátima, Portugal — the Cova da Iria, first anniversary of the attempt on his life
acts.object: The world, entrusted and consecrated to the Immaculate Heart
acts.text: A year to the day after being shot in Saint Peter's Square, John Paul II went to Fátima and repeated the act of entrustment of 7 June 1981. The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith describes it in exactly those terms — the 1981 act "repeated in Fatima on 13 May 1982". Russia is not named and the bishops of the world are not convoked; both would come two years later.

acts.place: Saint Peter's Square, Rome — before the image brought from the Capelinha at Fátima
acts.object: All men and women and all peoples, entrusted to the Immaculate Heart
acts.text: The act the argument is about. On 8 December 1983 the pope wrote to the bishops of the world asking them to join him; on 25 March 1984, in spiritual union with those bishops, "convoked" beforehand, he entrusted all men and women and all peoples to the Immaculate Heart of Mary. Russia is not named in the text. The collegial condition is satisfied and the naming condition is not, which is exactly why the act is disputed — and why the dispute is settled, for the Holy See, by testimony rather than by the text: Sister Lúcia wrote on 8 November 1989 that "yes it has been done just as Our Lady asked, on 25 March 1984", and the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, publishing that letter in 2000, added that "hence any further discussion or request is without basis". This page records the act, the letter and the Congregation's conclusion, and does not adjudicate between them and those who keep asking.
acts.quote: …we entrust and consecrate to you this very consecration of the world, placing it in your motherly Heart.

acts.place: Saint Peter's Square, Rome — Marian Day of the Year of Faith, before the original image brought from Fátima
acts.object: The Church and the world, entrusted to Our Lady of Fátima
acts.text: The image from the Capelinha was flown to Rome for the Marian Day of the Year of Faith and Francis made an act of entrustment before it. The word "consecrate" does not appear in the text, and neither the Immaculate Heart nor Russia is named — so the act is recorded here as what it calls itself, an "affidamento". It is in this section because it is routinely counted in the series, and the difference between being counted and being one is the kind of thing this section exists to keep visible.

acts.place: Saint Peter's Basilica, Rome — and simultaneously at Fátima, by the papal almoner
acts.object: The Church and all humanity, especially Russia and Ukraine
acts.text: A month into the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the only act in the series that satisfies both reported conditions in its own text: Russia is consecrated by name, and by the letter of 21 March the bishops of the world were invited to join. The Holy See did not present it as supplying anything missing from 1984 — the 2000 position that the request was fulfilled has not been withdrawn — and this page does not present it that way either. It records what the text says and lets the two columns be read side by side.
acts.quote: Therefore, Mother of God and our Mother, to your Immaculate Heart we solemnly entrust and consecrate ourselves, the Church and all humanity, especially Russia and Ukraine.
